To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of psychiatric disorders is high in children with ASD, and the prevalence of clinically impairing psychiatric disorders is higher still.
(1) most children with ASD are impaired by psychiatric symptoms, and (2) impairment and symptoms are highly correlated.

(1) the majority of children with ASD are impaired by symptoms of psychiatric disorders; (2) a substantial proportion of youth with ASD are impaired, yet do not meet criteria for any psychiatric disorder; and (3) impairment cutoffs are more sensitive and specific than symptom cutoffs for detecting psychiatric disorders in ASD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship of psychiatric symptoms to impairment and the implications of different methods of assessing impairment.
the prevalence and nature of psychiatric symptoms, their relation to functional impairment, and their relation to the presence of ASD.
the development of a new method for the assessment of the severity of psychiatric symptomatology in children with ASD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the prevalence and nature of psychiatric disorders in children with ASD are similar to those of non ASD children, but that the clinical expression of psychiatric disorders in ASD children is more likely to result in functional impairment.
psychiatric symptoms impair children with ASD in ways that are similar to and different from non ASD children.
impairment cutoff is a useful and necessary criterion for identifying youth with ASD who are in need of clinical attention and treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
psychiatric impairment in children with ASD is common and is not well captured using symptom cutoffs alone.

psychiatric symptom impairment in ASD is common, and is related to both the presence and severity of symptoms and other common parameters of child mental health, such as impairment, comorbidity, and family functioning.

psychiatric symptoms in youth with ASD are highly prevalent and impairing, and that impairment is a more valid and useful criterion than symptom counts for identifying youth who would be likely to benefit from treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
impairment is common in children with ASD and that the presence of impairment is related to the severity and number of symptoms.

the majority of children with ASD are impaired in their functioning by symptoms of at least one psychiatric condition, and this is true regardless of whether the symptoms meet symptom cutoff criteria for caseness.
impairment is a useful concept in the assessment of mental health problems in children with ASD.
